clinicalPearls: A painless autoimmune destructive thyroiditis causing transient thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism and usually recovery
Unlike subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis it is painless, and unlike Graves disease there is no ophthalmopathy
Radioactive iodine uptake is low during the thyrotoxic phase, distinguishing it from Graves disease
It is considered part of the autoimmune thyroid disease spectrum and is related to postpartum thyroiditis
The thyrotoxic phase is managed symptomatically with beta-blockade rather than antithyroid drugs
A minority develop permanent hypothyroidism, so follow-up thyroid function testing is needed
reference.pathophysiology: Silent thyroiditis is an autoimmune lymphocytic inflammation of the thyroid that transiently destroys follicular cells, releasing preformed thyroid hormone and causing a self-limited thyrotoxic phase. As stored hormone is depleted and the gland recovers, a hypothyroid phase often follows before euthyroidism is usually restored. Because the process is destructive rather than hyperfunctioning, radioactive iodine uptake is low, and antithyroid drugs are ineffective. It shares its autoimmune basis and biphasic course with postpartum thyroiditis.
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests through the phases
Thyroid radioactive iodine uptake (low in the thyrotoxic phase)
Inflammatory markers (usually normal, unlike subacute thyroiditis)
Follow-up thyroid function to detect permanent hypothyroidism
redFlags: Features suggesting Graves disease (ophthalmopathy) needing different management
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover normal thyroid function within months, though some develop permanent hypothyroidism and recurrence can occur.
pitfalls: Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs, which do not work in destructive thyroiditis
Misdiagnosing it as Graves disease and giving radioactive iodine
Failing to monitor for permanent hypothyroidism
Overlooking the link with the postpartum period
management: Symptomatic beta-blockade (such as propranolol) for adrenergic features of the thyrotoxic phase, since the process is destructive and antithyroid drugs are ineffective
Levothyroxine replacement during a symptomatic or prolonged hypothyroid phase, with a planned attempt at withdrawal once recovery is likely
Avoidance of radioiodine and thyroidectomy, given the self-limiting course and low radioiodine uptake
Serial thyroid function testing through the thyrotoxic, hypothyroid and recovery phases to track evolution and detect permanent hypothyroidism
Surveillance for recurrence, particularly in the postpartum setting given the shared autoimmune basis
Reassurance regarding the usually self-limiting nature of the illness
